extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners; patent prosecutors and applicants (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent applications under the AIA (first-inventor-to-file) provisions, explaining prior art categories (35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)/(2)), exceptions (35 U.S.C. 102(b)), effective filing date rules, and the obviousness standard (35 U.S.C. 103). Intended to be applied claim-by-claim in prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — "claimed invention" (35 U.S.C. 100(j))
rubrics_metrics.description: The term “claimed invention” is defined as the subject matter defined by a claim in a patent or an application for a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used throughout AIA 35 U.S.C. 102/103 analysis as the unit assessed against prior art and exceptions; applies on a claim-by-claim basis when determining effective filing date and prior art effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — "effective filing date" (35 U.S.C. 100(i)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: The “effective filing date” for a claimed invention is the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application containing the claimed invention; or (2) the filing date of the earliest provisional, nonprovisional, international (PCT), or foreign patent application to which the patent or application is entitled to benefit or priority as to such claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of prior art availability and applicability of AIA vs pre-AIA law turns on the effective filing date. Effective filing date is determined claim-by-claim and depends on satisfaction of support/112 requirements in earlier applications. See specific rules for continuation/divisional, CIP, provisional benefit (119(e)), and foreign priority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — "inventor" and "joint/coinventor" (35 U.S.C. 100(f), 100(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: The term “inventor” means the individual (or individuals collectively in a joint invention) who invented or discovered the subject matter of the invention; “joint inventor” and “coinventor” mean any one of the individuals who invented or discovered the subject matter of a joint invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant to determining whether disclosures were made by the inventor or obtained directly/indirectly from the inventor for purposes of AIA 102(b) exceptions and derivation/ownership inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art categories under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not patentable if it was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documents/activities that may be relied upon include issued patents, published applications, non-patent printed publications, evidence of public use, on-sale activities, or other public availability. A printed publication that lacks an early-enough date may still serve as evidence of an earlier public use or sale that qualifies as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art patent-document category under AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is not patentable if it was described in a U.S. patent, a U.S. patent application publication, or an application for patent deemed published under 35 U.S.C. 122(b) that names another inventor and was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WIPO publications of PCT applications that designate the United States are treated as U.S. patent application publications for prior-art purposes regardless of international filing/publication language or whether the PCT application enters U.S. national stage. A U.S. patent document’s prior-art date is its effective filing date as determined under 35 U.S.C. 102(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA one-year grace period — exceptions under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(1) if (A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or a joint inventor or by another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor; or (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor or joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effectively provides a one-year grace period after an inventor-originated disclosure during which a patent application may be filed and not be barred by that disclosure. The one-year period is measured from the filing date of the earliest application to which benefit/priority is properly claimed and which supports the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). The end date is extended to the next business day if it falls on a weekend or federal holiday (35 U.S.C. 21(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement of the one-year grace period (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The one-year grace period in AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(1) is measured from the filing date of any U.S. or foreign patent application to which the patent or application is entitled to benefit or priority as to such invention, provided the earlier application supports the claimed invention as required by 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differs from pre-AIA grace period measurement (which measured from earliest U.S. filing date); applies irrespective of whether the earlier application was filed in the U.S. or abroad. See MPEP §§ 2153.01(a), 2153.02 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to 102(a)(2) under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure shall not be prior art under subsection (a)(2) if (A) the subject matter disclosed was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or joint inventor; (B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or a joint inventor or another who obtained the subject matter from the inventor or joint inventor; or (C) the subject matter disclosed and the claimed invention, not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention, were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These exceptions protect inventor-originated disclosures and commonly-owned subject matter from being treated as intervening U.S. patent-document prior art under 102(a)(2). They do not, however, except disclosures that qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) (e.g., public uses or publications by others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-ownership exception (102(b)(2)(C)) — scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure in a U.S. patent document is not prior art under 102(a)(2) if the disclosed subject matter and the claimed invention were owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person not later than the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replaces pre-AIA 103(c) limited exception and applies to prior patents/published applications of co-workers/collaborators for both novelty (102) and nonobviousness (103) purposes when the conditions are met. It does not remove a disclosure as prior art under 102(a)(1); a coworker disclosure that is publicly available remains prior art under 102(a)(1) unless it fits a 102(b)(1) exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint research agreement deemed common ownership (102(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter disclosed and a claimed invention shall be deemed to have been owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person for 102(b)(2)(C) purposes if: (1) the subject matter disclosed was developed and the claimed invention was made by, or on behalf of, one or more parties to a joint research agreement that was in effect on or before the effective filing date; (2) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (3) the application for patent discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires a written contract/grant/cooperative agreement and satisfies the deemed-common-ownership condition only when all three predicate conditions are met; see 35 U.S.C. 100(h) definition of joint research agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. patent document "effectively filed" as prior art (102(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A U.S. patent document is considered to have been effectively filed for prior-art purposes on the earlier of: (1) the actual filing date of the patent or application; or (2) the filing date of the earliest application to which the patent or application is entitled to claim benefit or priority and that describes the subject matter relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a U.S. patent document is effective as prior art as of the filing date of the earliest application to which benefit/priority is claimed and which describes the relied-upon subject matter, whether that earliest application is a U.S. provisional/nonprovisional, an international (PCT) application, or a foreign patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global view of prior art — no geographic requirement under AIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the AIA, prior public use, sale activity, or other disclosure has no geographic requirement (i.e., need not be in the United States) to qualify as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differs from pre-AIA rules that required certain activities to occur in the United States to qualify as prior art. Applies to 102(a)(1) activities (patented, printed publication, public use, on sale, otherwise available).

rubrics_metrics.name: "Described" for anticipation under 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) — elements and enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: For a prior art document to ‘describe’ a claimed invention such that it anticipates under 102, it must disclose “each and every element of the claimed invention” either explicitly or inherently, with the elements arranged or combined as in the claim, and a person of ordinary skill in the art must have been enabled to make the invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The description requirement for anticipation is distinct from the written-description/enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A prior art reference need not satisfy the 112(a) "how to use" requirement and can anticipate even if it does not disclose a use or reduce the invention to practice. Case law cited: In re Gleave; Eli Lilly; Net MoneyIN; In re Bond; Impax Labs; In re LeGrice; In re Donohue; In re Schoenwald; Schering Corp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication may be evidence of earlier public use/sale
rubrics_metrics.description: A printed publication that does not have a sufficiently early publication date to qualify as prior art under 102(a)(1) may nonetheless be competent evidence of a previous public use, sale activity, or other availability of the claimed invention to the public where the public use or sale does have a sufficiently early date to qualify as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office may rely on non-patent literature as supporting evidence for earlier public activities (see In re Epstein and MPEP § 2133.03(b)). Examiners should consider such evidentiary uses when publication date itself is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard under AIA 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent may not be obtained if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal focus under AIA is the effective filing date (not date of invention). AIA 103 also states patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. Pre-AIA 103(c) provisions replaced by 102(b)(2)(C) and (c); pre-AIA 103(b) biotech process provisions eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination/continuing applicability of certain pre-AIA provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The AIA eliminates the provisions in pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(c) (abandonment), 102(f) (naming wrong inventor), and 102(g) (prior invention by another), subject to limited applicability in mixed-date applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situations such as incorrect named inventors are now handled by derivation proceedings (35 U.S.C. 135), correction of inventorship under 37 CFR 1.48, or by rejections under 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115. Pre-AIA 102(g) still applies to claims with effective filing dates before March 16, 2013, or in applications that ever claimed benefit of earlier filings having pre-March 16, 2013 effective dates; see MPEP § 2138 and form paragraph references.

rubrics_metrics.name: AIA effective/applicability date and definition of an AIA application
rubrics_metrics.description: AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103 took effect March 16, 2013 and apply to any patent application that contains or contained at any time a claim to a claimed invention that has an effective filing date on or after March 16, 2013, or that is designated as a continuation/divisional/CIP of an application containing such a claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such applications are referred to as AIA (first-inventor-to-file) applications. Where an application includes claims with both pre- and post-March 16, 2013 effective filing dates, the AIA’s provisions apply to the claims having effective filing dates on/after March 16, 2013; pre-AIA rules may still apply to other claims (see MPEP § 2159 et seq.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim determination of effective filing date
rubrics_metrics.description: The effective filing date of a claimed invention is determined on a claim-by-claim basis and not on an application-by-application basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different claims in the same application may be entitled to different effective filing dates (e.g., due to support in parent applications, CIP new matter, provisional support). Prior art is applied on a claim-by-claim basis, but whether pre-AIA or AIA statutes apply is determined on an application-by-application basis per MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office's burden and procedural notice requirements (35 U.S.C. 132; 37 CFR 1.104(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office bears the initial burden of explaining why applicable statutory/regulatory requirements have not been met when rejecting a claim; whenever a claim is rejected or an objection/requirement is made, the Office shall notify the applicant and state the reasons and provide information and references useful to judging whether to continue prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must state the reasons for rejections and provide useful references per statutory/regulatory requirements; this procedural rule remains unchanged under the AIA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent grant date as prior-art date for "patented" (102(a)(1)) and secret patent exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claimed invention was patented before the effective filing date, the patent’s grant date is the applicable prior-art date for purposes of 102(a)(1), except where the patent was secret as of the date rights were awarded — in that case the patent is available as prior art as of the date it was made available to the public (e.g., laid open for public inspection or disseminated in printed form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See In re Ekenstam and In re Carlson for examples. Examiners should use the grant date as prior-art date unless facts show the patent was not publicly available until later.
